summary: Bee is an AI wearable microphone that records everything a user says, building a personal AI agent and extracting data for third-party systems. Steve Korshakov estimates a single person captures about 10 million tokens per year, and within one week of wearing the device, virtually everything about that person can be learned, making it arguably the most sensitive capture device on the market. The mission was to ensure no one at Amazon can access this data. Being inside Amazon made this harder: a typical AWS customer trusts Amazon to see their data, but Bee had to defend against Amazon itself as a potential insider threat. The system rests on four core principles. First, the encryption key lives only on the user's phone (iPhone or Android) and is never persisted by Bee. Second, everything is encrypted with no opt-out or bypass. Third, all workloads are fully transparent and audited. Fourth, trust dependencies are minimized. Key management works as follows: the phone holds the key, connects to the backend, and runs an attestation pipeline verifying that the specific workload matches a public transparency log using Sigstore. Anyone can verify the workload is genuine. After attestation, the client shares the key with backend nodes running inside confidential compute. Bee runs its own inference rather than relying on third-party API providers, and code is replicated only to specific nodes, limiting scope. Keys in memory have a forced seven-day expiration, chosen as a realistic time horizon for useful agent work. For production deployments, a two-tier signing system prevents insiders from shipping compromised code unnoticed. A dedicated Amazon privacy team, separate from Bee, holds signing keys hardcoded into client apps and backends. Bee can influence but cannot control this team, and very high-level employees must sign off on changes. The deployment process splits into building a base image and then deploying a manifest to the transparency log. After VM self-verification, a certificate is issued embedding all attestation and transparency proofs; they use a private CA because public certificates would populate a public transparency log. The entire system is about 20,000 lines of memory-safe code, most of it just verifying attestation, with no homegrown cryptography—Korshakov explicitly contrasts this with his Telegram experience where building custom crypto was a mistake. On taming agents, he says sandboxing and limiting what agents can do is the only approach that works; nothing else reliably prevents harmful behavior.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The most sensitive capture device on the market
sections.summary: Korshakov introduces Bee, an AI wearable microphone that records everything and builds a personal agent. He quantifies the sensitivity: ~10 million tokens per person per year, and within one week virtually everything about the person can be learned, making it one of the most sensitive capture devices on the market.

sections.title: The mission: no one, not even Amazon, can read your data
sections.summary: Because the data is so sensitive, Bee encrypted everything with the mission that no one at Amazon can access it. Being inside Amazon made this harder because Amazon normally provides guarantees as a customer that they can see your data, so Bee needed additional protection against internal threats.

sections.title: Why the agent runs continuously, not request-response
sections.summary: Bee believes agents should work continuously, not just in request-response mode. They built a stateful runtime with persistent memory that can connect to tools and third-party services, run autonomously without the user device being online, yet remain fully controlled by the user. This is framed as a glimpse into how personal agents will evolve.

sections.title: Four principles: the key never leaves your phone
sections.summary: The encryption system rests on four core ideas: the key is managed only on the customer's phone and never persisted by Bee; everything is encrypted with no opt-out or bypass; all workloads are fully transparent and audited; and trust dependencies are minimized.

sections.title: Attestation and a public transparency log
sections.summary: Key management starts with the phone holding the key and connecting to the backend. The phone runs a sophisticated attestation pipeline verifying workload integrity and that the workload is in a public transparency log (Sigstore). Anyone can verify the workload is genuine. After attestation, the client shares the key with backend nodes in confidential compute.

sections.title: Own inference, confidential compute, and 7-day keys
sections.summary: Bee runs its own inference inside confidential compute, a more complex task than typical AI companies face. Code is replicated only to specific nodes, limiting scope. Keys in memory have a forced seven-day expiration, chosen because 24 hours is too low—users may not open their phone within that window and useful work would be missed.

sections.title: Signing so no insider can ship unnoticed
sections.summary: To prevent insiders from shipping compromised code, Bee uses a two-tier signing system. A dedicated Amazon privacy team, separate from Bee, manages the transparency log and signing keys, which are hardcoded into client apps and backends. Bee can influence but not control this team. High-level employees must sign off on changes. Deployment splits into building a base image and deploying a manifest to the transparency log.

sections.title: Certificates that embed the proofs
sections.summary: After VM self-verification, a certificate is issued embedding all attestation and transparency proofs. They use a private CA because public certificates would populate a public transparency log. They may introduce an extra proxy for normal TLS with lighter attestation, but this does not exist yet.

sections.title: Q&A: joining Amazon, 20k lines, and taming agents
sections.summary: In Q&A, Korshakov explains that joining Amazon required protecting against internal threats since Amazon normally can see customer data. They use normal EC2 instances. The system is about 20,000 lines of memory-safe code, mostly attestation verification, with no homegrown crypto—deliberately avoiding a mistake he made at Telegram. On taming agents, he says sandboxing is the only reliable approach; everything else fails.
